story_text.value:
Hi HN, I built Nexus because I was tired of having multiple agents that I had to address one by one. I built an underlying mechanism where I could message all of them and have them have the capability to message each other and listen to wake events. I also got tired of having to run cron when I think that agents should have the capability to be event-driven.

Nexus is basically a daemon that runs and routes messages to where they need to be, it is fully customizable, which you can write scripts off of so that it will wake agents or route that message to an already existing agent. Right now it supports Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode and Hermes. But more are underway. It runs on your machine with no container required. (In my opinion, messaging within your machine should not require you to have to run a container.)

To try it:

  npm install --global @egregore/nexus
It runs on Linux, Windows and WSL today; It can run on mac but I havent fully tested it also you would have to build the binaries yourself for the latest version though. Full support for it is planned in the near future.

story_text.value:
We noticed during the course of many many years of DBA related work that fixes to database issues and queries are always reactive. An entire database can fall over extremely quickly when an unbounded query grows without warning.

Traditionally, DBAs hear complaints of slowness and follow a methodical process: - manually browse pg_stats or other database related performance internal tables - see which queries are slowest - figure out what indexes are missing - figure out which indexes are actually bad and slowing down writes - painstakingly implement a fix

In the age of cheap intelligence, we decided that there is no reason we can’t have an always-on agent that is designed to do this job for you. Databases need something or someone that is always watching with a massive amount of contextual understanding to be able to take quick actions. We’ve watched the alternative play out repeatedly. One of our users’s checkout page went from loading instantly to taking 11 seconds in a single night with no code change. How? Well somehow their order table grew by 40M rows because BI team had injected historical data and suddenly postgres started doing full table scans. Sometimes routine operations have unintended results and can easily destroy your database. We wanted to catch these kinds of regressions instantly. So we built RDST.

RDST is a desktop agent that runs on your PC and connects to PostgreSQL / MYSQL (read only) and compares every query against its own performance every minute. Every expensive query is automatically EXPLAIN ANALYZED, stripped of PII and sent to U.S. based frontier or open model providers to analyze which indexes are missing, how the query could be rewritten, and provides the fix. We then run a classifier model (JEV) to decide if you should be notified (is this standard behavior for this particular query?), and the full history of the query performance is kept for years. RDST also keeps track of your entire database health in general, and recommends more fixes than simply bad queries.

Since it runs locally we can keep the database credentials stored in your OS Keychain (RDST never keeps them in its own storage layer), and the connection goes straight to your database (using a jump host or SSH tunnel for private connections). You can read more about how we handle data especially as it pertains to LLM use here.

https://readyset.io/docs/readyset-ai/rdst/desktop/privacy

We really want feedback from the community from people running Postgres and MySQL in production. We are giving inference away completely for free.

Just as a reminder, RDST will NOT run any updates or indexes against your database at this time. We are considering a fully autonomous auto-pilot mode in the future, but for now we are leaving the actual fixes in your hands.

Let us know what you think!

story_text.value:
sys2txt is a command line tool that records whatever audio your Linux machine is playing (via PulseAudio/PipeWire's monitor source) and transcribes it live with Whisper, OpenAI's AI-based speech-to-text model.

I use it to caption meetings, videos, and calls playing on my own machine without routing audio through anything else. It supports faster-whisper, openai-whisper, and whisper.cpp (with Vulkan GPU support for AMD), and can either record-then-transcribe once or stream continuously in segments with live output in txt/srt/vtt/json/tsv.

I'd be keen to collaborate with others extend its functionality to other operating systems and hardware.

(I have been using and developing this tool since November 2025.)

story_text.value:
I noticed that a lot of non-technical people don’t use AI to its full extent. Like they use the wrong model for the task, the wrong reasoning effort, or vague prompts. That gap between "what the AI can do" and "what people actually get" is what I wanted to fix.

So I spent the last two years in my spare time building a consumer AI product that tries to fix this issue.

This is how it works: When it receives the request, an LLM decides the task type (chat, reasoning, coding, writing) and the tool calls that are needed (web search, image generation, video generation, audio generation). Then it routes it to a suitable model and applies a prompt based on the task type. If it's a media generation task, it rewrites the prompt into a detailed one using prompt formulas (the prompt formulas for specific styles are mentioned in the system prompt). The LLM that is used for answering the request can also use a map, generate a mermaid diagram, generate a quiz or flashcards, generate files, etc.

A limitation right now is that routing adds latency, but I'm currently experimenting with decision-models like Jev, PPLX Decider, etc. and might use decision-models to route to the right LLM and give the tool calls like web search and media generation to the answering LLM.

It launched this week, so it's still early and I will keep improving it and adding new things.

Also sign-up/in is required to prevent abuse.

I’d really like honest feedback: what’s confusing, what’s missing, etc.

Partition aware, agg aware, and compute engine aware semantic routing.

Please send feedbacks and issues on Github.

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

In Keen Code, a coding agent solo-developed by me, I have implemented a task-classifier using Jev and a simple auto-router based on the classification result. The article shares details about how it's implemented.

In short, it has a very simple idea:

- For every user message, ask Jev to classify the task in one of the three categories (simple, standard, complex) given current state of the conversation.

- Keen also asks Jev to put a probability on this question: "is this a new task?"

- Based on the result, Keen uses a heuristic to switch the current model to one of the three pre-configured models by user for the three categories

- To make the router work, users have to configure one model per task category inside the coding agent itself

The heuristic is also very simple:

When routing is enabled, Keen switches only if the selected-category probability is greater than 0.5 and either:

- new-task probability is at least 0.6; or - category probability is greater than 0.8 and the target category is a higher tier than the active routed model.

Thoughts and feedback are welcome. And if you are interested to know more about Keen Code, the repo can be found here: https://github.com/mochow13/keen-code

story_text.value:
Hey HN, this is Andy from Respan (https://www.respan.ai). We are building an open-source Rust AI gateway. It is a decoupled gateway, so everything is a plugin, including different providers, protocols (MCP, voice), modalities (images, videos), and gateway features (fallbacks, PII redaction, smart routing).

Instead of packaging tons of providers and features into one gateway, Respan provides a small core and public interfaces that teams can use to assemble the AI infrastructure their application needs. That way, users can build their own features as additional plugins without having to change the gateway's core.

Here’s a video demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVv2ibXiTXM

There are countless LLM gateways and most of them solve a common problem: calling different providers from a single endpoint. However, adding new features can become prohibitively difficult. So developers can end up building another gateway to solve a specific problem.

We've been building our gateway based on LiteLLM since 2024, and now it's providing services for thousands of orgs. Each org needs different API key settings, routes, and limits. To support that, we kept wrapping LiteLLM, adding more features to it, and at one stage, our wrapper code exceeded 100,000 lines.

This January, a routine LiteLLM upgrade caused intermittent connection errors, and we had to roll back. We still haven't figured out the cause, but since then, we no longer upgrade LiteLLM directly and instead manually backport upstream fixes. These experiences made us realize that continuing to patch LiteLLM is not a sustainable long-term solution, and we had to redesign the gateway ourselves.

While redesigning our gateway, we wanted to make it easier to add features without breaking existing ones. Inspired by Nginx, we think an AI gateway should have a really small core, only responsible for dispatching events.

We believe that everything should be a plugin in our gateway, including providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini), protocols (chat, realtime voice, MCP), modalities (images, videos), and gateway features for reliability and security (smart routing, fallbacks, and PII redaction through example plugins). Beyond that, we want developers to be able to easily extend the gateway's capabilities by adding their own plugins, without touching the core. Adding a provider, even your own, is dead simple, because quirks are plugins too and there’s nothing magical about them. A provider is a short file, Mistral’s is 22 lines, and each quirk, like Groq putting token usage in its own field, gets its own test.

Respan Gateway does more than let you call Claude or Gemini models from the OpenAI SDK. It handles tools, images, and reasoning protocols automatically: an application based on the OpenAI Realtime API can also use Gemini Live through the gateway, though not every feature translates. A simple chat app can use MCP tools configured in the gateway, without implementing MCP itself.

We also parse requests into a shared structure. When the client and provider use the same API, we preserve provider-specific fields in their native format, even if our shared structure doesn't have a field for them. That way, the gateway can write them back instead of dropping them.

Here’s how it works:

An adapter hands each HTTP or WebSocket connection to the first client format that recognizes it. The format exposes the request as a two-way stream of typed input and output events. The core runs plugins in registration order, allowing them to choose a provider, filter or wrap either stream, make additional calls, return a response, or refuse the request. A provider format then opens the upstream connection.

If the client and provider use the same format and no plugin changes the payload, the original bytes and protocol-specific fields can pass through unchanged. When formats differ, they translate through shared types for messages, tool calls, results, streams, and usage. This stream model can represent both one-shot HTTP requests and long-lived bidirectional sessions.

The gateway is open source at https://github.com/respanai/respan-gateway under the MIT or Apache-2.0 license. You don't need to use Respan's hosted platform and can run it directly on your local machine. Build it from source, add your provider keys, and swap the base URL in a supported client. You can keep using the API your client already speaks. It's still pre-alpha.

We make money from our hosted platform (https://www.respan.ai/pricing), which runs the gateway for you with native observability and evals, along with unified billing.

If you’re building routing, tools, filtering, observability, or security for agents, we'd love to see it as a plugin. PLUGINS.md in the repo explains how to write one and links to the plugins we’ve created so far. Turning that into an ecosystem is basically our roadmap, and we welcome you to contribute your own plugins. We'd love to answer any questions and hear your feedback!

https://github.com/respanai/respan-gateway

story_text.value:
What’s up HN?! I'm Benji, and I’ve been building Frink since ~April this year.

Frink is a desktop-first, open-source (MIT) app for running coding agents in parallel and multi-step workflows that start on their own. It runs on your machine (macOS and Linux) with your own provider login. It currently supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, and OpenCode, but the latter 3 are in preview. No Frink account to use the app.

The biggest USP of Frink is workflows: think n8n for agents. You describe a routine in a sentence, for example: "every weekday at 9am, run the tests; if any fail, have an agent fix them, then wait for my approval before it opens a PR." Then, Frink builds it as a workflow (or simply, Flow): a list of steps you can read and change before it runs. A Flow can start on a schedule, from any webhook, or from an event from a third-party such as Linear, Shortcut, ClickUp, Sentry, PostHog, etc. Steps can be agent turns, shell commands, conditions, approval steps that stop and wait for you, or steps you write yourself in code (or ask the agent to write one). Everything that needs you (an approval, an agent's question, a finished task to review) lands in one Work Queue.

Other stuff:

* Up to four agents side by side, each on its own git worktree if you want. Or, many agents out of direct view.

* Every change shows as a diff; there's a code editor, a terminal, etc.

* Local-first: chats, Flows and tasks live in SQLite on your machine.

* Easier provider parity: currently working on and improving the tooling setup between providers. Once inside Frink, irrespective of what provider you use, the hooks, MCPs, and other tooling work out of the box between providers.

Why I built it: I started building it when there weren’t many other competitors; now the industry is swamped with ADEs and harnesses. However, in my opinion, each still lacks good automation for more fine-tuned scenarios. I doubled down on the flows to help me with my actual day-to-day job as a SWE, and over time it’s helped me automate most of the PRs being shipped across my personal projects, team, etc., to the point that it’s a continuous loop and helps a whole ton.

Notes: Windows isn't supported yet. Flows only run on Claude Code and Codex for now. It's a solo project, so expect sharp edges.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Faithful. I built dánwò, an open-source (Apache-2.0) end-to-end testing framework for web and mobile apps, written in TypeScript.

The problem: a UI test can click "Pay", see "Payment successful" and pass, while the card was charged twice, the webhook was handled twice, or the receipt email never went out. With coding agents writing more of our code, that gap between "the screen looks right" and "the right things happened" is where I kept finding bugs.

How it works:

- Tests drive the app like a user, with locators or plain-English agent steps. An agent step calls a model once; danwo records the actions and replays them on later runs with no model calls, so CI doesn't need an API key.

- Your app runs behind an egress proxy. Calls to Stripe, Clerk, Resend, Slack, Google and about 20 other providers are answered by local emulators at the real hostnames, so there are no sandbox keys and no code changes. For Node apps a preload routes the calls; Bun honours HTTPS_PROXY.

- An invariant is a check that runs after the test and compares two sides: what the provider says happened (charges, emails, messages) and what your app stored. For example, credits granted must equal paid checkouts times 500.

- `danwo matrix` replays a test once per fault it could meet: a 500 or 429 from a provider, a declined card, a duplicate, late, forged or replayed webhook, a double-submit, a database commit whose reply is lost, Postgres unreachable for a few seconds. The invariant judges every run, so you see exactly which failure your app mishandles.

- Every run leaves a flight record: video, each step, every provider call, webhook delivery and database statement, with secrets redacted.

It runs in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, and on the Android emulator and iOS Simulator. It ships an MCP server and a skill, so coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) can write and run tests and fix what fails.

Limitations, honestly: the emulators are only as good as their fidelity to the real APIs. Each one has a suite that runs against the real provider to catch drift, but they won't cover every edge of Stripe's API. Backend routing is built for Node and Bun today. Mobile tests need macOS or Linux. It's early (v0.1.2).

The name is Yorùbá: "dán an wò" means "try it and see".

Quickstart: npx @danwo/cli init (docs: https://danwo.dev/docs/quickstart)

I'd love feedback, especially on faults you've been bitten by that aren't in the matrix yet.

story_text.value:
Wrote everything myself from scratch in pure C without any Linux or pre-built distros. It's a custom monolithic architecture with the Limine bootloader, custom drivers, window manager, and terminal.

As for models and agents: I used LLM agents as co-authors for routine tasks, writing tests, and debugging low-level code. I tuned them to strictly generate code without the standard library (libc) and to create host-side unit tests to verify modules before packing them into the kernel.

https://github.com/AnonimusShamshiAlex/LimonOS
